source.title: Effects of sparsity and superposition on loss in simple autoencoders
source.citation: Mriganka Basu Roy Chowdhury et al., 2026
source.authors: Mriganka Basu Roy Chowdhury; Eric M. Weiner

record.file_problem: No apparent truncation or wrong-document problem; the text is readable, though some mathematical notation has extraction artifacts.
record.tranche_reason: The paper gives theoretical bounds and a constructed low-coherence representation for the same toy-autoencoder superposition question, rather than reproducing the original empirical method.
record.gate_note: The paper's references to LLMs, sparse autoencoders, and prior superposition results are not results of this study. Figure 3 reports numerical optimization curves, but exact plotted values are not stated in the text.
record.test_reason: Proofs, not training, address the original toy-autoencoder question. For power activations and p ≤ d^-m, the optimal objective is Θ(pd^m). Unsuperposed and linear solutions are capped at Θ(pd). So optimal solutions must be superposed, and the gain depends on sparsity.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also frame the bounds as rigorously corroborating Elhage et al.'s finding that superposition helps under sparsity with nonlinearity. They note the O(d) upper bound may be loose. They doubt gradient descent finds the highly structured construction.
record.recipe_differences: The authors say their tied-weight, one-layer autoencoder is almost identical to the original toy model, with minor modifications for analysis. This paper focuses on theoretical loss bounds and a constructed matrix, uses power activations and equal feature importance, and does not establish training outcomes.
record.method_sensitivity: The bounds and construction depend on sparsity p, hidden dimension d, activation power m, and, for the O(d) upper bound, a strong log-concavity assumption. Numerical curves are shown for d=10 and d=15 with m=3.
record.problems: The paper states that the true order of the optimum remains open and that the O(d) upper bound may be loose. The numerical optimization examples use d=10 and d=15 and leave the larger-p behavior ambiguous. The paper does not determine whether gradient descent converges to the constructed structured solutions; it lists this as an open problem. Results are for the equal-importance case.

untested.parts: What gradient-trained networks actually learn (the authors doubt they converge to the construction), the regular geometries of learned solutions, the location or sharpness of a phase transition at intermediate sparsity, and unequal feature importance.
All of it: equal importance is assumed and no neurons are measured.
All of it: no LLMs or SAEs.
All of it: no comparison of 1-D and multi-dimensional features.

missing.what: First-order (very sparse) objective F(B) is at most d^m, and the Lemma 4.1 construction attains this up to constants. This ties near-orthogonal geometry to the optimum.
Theorem 3.2 extends the O(d) upper bound to non-i.i.d. strongly log-concave inputs with arbitrary sparsity patterns.

record.verdict_notes: This is a pure theory paper, apart from small numerical optimizations (d=10 and 15, m=3). Its evidence for V1 concerns optimal loss under superposition, not the learned geometry. The reader's V6 link is unwarranted.

versions.untested_parts: The paper analyzes optimal reconstruction loss and gives a low-coherence construction, but does not establish what trained networks learn, a general sparsity-dependent geometry transition, or regular geometries of learned solutions.
The paper assumes equal feature importance and does not measure neuron polysemanticity or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions while others share.
No alternative causes of polysemantic neurons are studied.
No LLM activations, neurons, or dictionary features are measured.
No SAE feature completeness, stability, or canonical status is tested.
The paper constructs a representation using vectors for scalar input coordinates, but does not compare one-dimensional directions against multidimensional feature representations.

rows.operation_detail: Theorem 2.2 bounds the supremum of the modified reconstruction objective over weights W.

conditions.value: p-sparse, independent coordinates with symmetric mean-zero distribution µ

rows.measure: sup_W L̃(W), the maximized modified squared-L2 reconstruction objective
rows.baseline: unsuperposed optimum Θ(pd), as stated in equations (9)–(10)
rows.value: C1 min(p d^m, d p^(1/m)) ≤ sup_W L̃(W) ≤ C2 p d^m
rows.note: For p≤d^-m the lower bound is C1 p d^m; the result concerns optimal objective value and does not itself identify the geometry of learned weights.
rows.check: State should be observed, not cannot_determine. The optimum exceeds the unsuperposed Θ(pd) baseline (r3) by a factor d^(m-1) when p ≤ d^-m. That implies the optimal W has non-orthogonal columns. The baseline field correctly cites eqs (9)–(10). The geometry of the optimum itself is not characterized.

rows.check: The O(d) upper bound shows the superposition advantage shrinks toward the unsuperposed level as p→1. This fits a sparsity-dependent benefit, but the bounds are not tight at intermediate p, so no transition is located.

relationships.condition: Theoretical optimum of the tied-weight one-layer autoencoder, odd power activations, equal importance, very sparse regime (p ≤ d^-m)
relationships.reason: The optimum is Θ(pd^m), versus Θ(pd) for unsuperposed or linear solutions, so optimal solutions superpose. Nearly orthogonal constructions attain it (r1, r4, r5). The advantage shrinks as p→1 (r2).
relationships.display_finding: For odd power activations with m>1, the optimum scaled as Θ(pd^m), against Θ(pd) for unsuperposed or linear solutions, so optimal solutions superpose, and nearly orthogonal constructions attain the optimum. The advantage shrank as p approached 1.
